title: Snowflake architecture
summary: How Snowflake separates storage, compute and services, stores data in micro-partitions, and uses caches, time travel and cloning.

blocks.text: Snowflake is a managed SQL data platform built on cloud object storage. Understanding its three layers explains almost every performance, cost and design decision you make on it, and maps directly onto the lakehouse ideas of Part V.
26.1 Three layers

blocks.title: Snowflake layers

layers.label: Cloud services
layers.sub: auth, metadata, optimizer, transactions, access control, result cache

layers.label: Compute: virtual warehouses
layers.sub: independent MPP clusters, local SSD cache, billed per second

layers.label: Storage
layers.sub: compressed columnar micro-partitions in cloud object storage

blocks.caption: Every warehouse reads the same storage; services coordinate them.

items: **Storage** holds tables as immutable micro-partitions in the cloud provider's object storage, managed entirely by Snowflake. You pay per TB-month of compressed data, including time travel and fail-safe copies.
**Compute** is a set of virtual warehouses. Each is an isolated cluster; two warehouses querying the same table do not compete for CPU. You pay credits while a warehouse runs.

**Cloud services** compile and optimize queries, keep all metadata (including micro-partition statistics), manage transactions and security. Its usage is billed only above a daily allowance relative to warehouse usage (historically 10%; check current terms).

blocks.text: 26.2 Micro-partitions and pruning

Every table is stored as micro-partitions: immutable files holding roughly 50 to 500 MB of uncompressed data, organized column by column and compressed per column. Snowflake creates them automatically in insertion order; you never declare partitions. For each micro-partition the services layer records per-column min/max values, distinct counts and null counts.

At compile time the optimizer compares predicates with these ranges and skips micro-partitions that cannot match, exactly the way Iceberg prunes files by manifest statistics (chapter 22). The query profile shows 'partitions scanned' against 'partitions total'; that ratio is the first thing to check on a slow query. DML never edits a micro-partition: an UPDATE writes new micro-partitions and retires the old ones, which is what makes time travel possible.

Pruning also happens at run time for joins: filters derived from the build side of a join can skip micro-partitions on the probe side. A selective dimension filter on a well-clustered fact table can therefore be very cheap.
26.3 Clustering

Natural insertion order often clusters data well on load time and badly on everything else. A **clustering key** tells Snowflake which columns to keep co-located. **Automatic clustering** then reclusters in the background with serverless compute billed separately, rewriting micro-partitions until overlap on the key is low.

blocks.title: Snowflake SQL

items: Worth it for large tables (typically multi-TB) where queries filter on columns not correlated with load order.
Choose few columns, lowest cardinality first; wrap timestamps in a date or truncation expression so the key is not near-unique.
Frequently updated tables recluster constantly: watch the automatic clustering cost before enabling it.
Search optimization is a separate paid service for selective point lookups and substring searches; clustering is about range pruning.

blocks.text: 26.4 Virtual warehouses

head: Size
Credits per hour
Rule of thumb
rows: Very large scans; check current sizes and generations

blocks.text: Each size step doubles compute and credit rate. For scan-heavy work that parallelizes well, a size up roughly halves runtime, so cost stays about the same and latency drops. Billing is per second with a minimum of 60 seconds each time a warehouse resumes. A warehouse that spills to local disk and then to remote storage (visible in the query profile) is undersized for that query.
Multi-cluster warehouses and concurrency

Size addresses heavy queries; **multi-cluster** addresses many concurrent queries. A multi-cluster warehouse (an Enterprise edition feature) has `MIN_CLUSTER_COUNT` and `MAX_CLUSTER_COUNT`. When queries queue, Snowflake starts more clusters of the same size. `SCALING_POLICY = STANDARD` adds clusters quickly to avoid queuing; `ECONOMY` waits until a new cluster would be kept busy, accepting some queuing to save credits.

blocks.title: Snowflake SQL: a BI warehouse
blocks.text:
CREATE WAREHOUSE bi_wh
  WAREHOUSE_SIZE    = 'SMALL'
  MIN_CLUSTER_COUNT = 1
  MAX_CLUSTER_COUNT = 4
  SCALING_POLICY    = 'STANDARD'
  AUTO_SUSPEND      = 60
  AUTO_RESUME       = TRUE;
26.5 Three caches

head: Cache
Where
What it saves
Invalidated by
rows: Whole query result, reused for an identical query by a role with access; no warehouse needed
Changes to underlying data, non-deterministic functions; expires 24 h after last use (up to 31 days)
Answers like COUNT(*), MIN/MAX on some columns straight from micro-partition stats
Local SSD of a running warehouse

blocks.text: Aggressive auto-suspend saves credits but drops the warehouse cache. For a BI warehouse serving the same dashboards all day, a suspend of a few minutes can be cheaper overall than 60 seconds; measure with query history rather than guessing.
26.6 Time travel, fail-safe and zero-copy cloning

Because micro-partitions are immutable, Snowflake keeps retired ones for a retention period. **Time travel** (`DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS`, default 1 day, up to 90 days for permanent tables on Enterprise edition) lets you query, clone or undrop past states. After that, permanent tables enter a 7-day **fail-safe** that only Snowflake support can recover from. Transient and temporary tables have at most 1 day of time travel and no fail-safe, which is cheaper for staging data you can rebuild.

blocks.title: Snowflake SQL: time travel and cloning

blocks.text: A **clone** is a metadata operation: the new object points at the same micro-partitions. Storage is only consumed as the clone or the original diverge. This makes full-size development and test environments, and pre-release backups, nearly free to create.

blocks.title: Recovering from a bad deployment
blocks.text: A transformation release overwrote a gold table with wrong currency conversions at 09:12. The team cloned the table `BEFORE (STATEMENT => ...)` the faulty statement into a side table, verified totals against finance, and swapped it in with `ALTER TABLE ... SWAP WITH`. Recovery took 15 minutes and copied no data.

blocks.title: Size and configure warehouses
blocks.text: A company has three workloads: nightly dbt transformations (2 hours on a Large warehouse, spilling to remote storage), a BI tool with 80 analysts peaking 9-11 a.m., and ad hoc data science queries scanning 5 TB tables. Propose warehouses (size, cluster counts, scaling policy, auto-suspend) and decide which large tables deserve clustering keys.
hints: Which workload is limited by query size, and which by concurrency?
What does remote spilling tell you about the dbt warehouse?
Which filters appear in the slowest queries, and do they match load order?

items: Storage, compute and cloud services scale and bill independently.
Tables are stored as immutable micro-partitions with per-column stats used for pruning.
Clustering keys and automatic clustering improve pruning on large tables at a serverless cost.
Warehouse size helps heavy queries; multi-cluster helps concurrency; billing is per second after a 60-second minimum.
Result, metadata and warehouse caches avoid work at different layers.
Time travel, fail-safe and zero-copy cloning all follow from immutable micro-partitions.

blocks.q: Fifty analysts run small dashboard queries at once and queries queue. What should you change first?
options: Add a clustering key to every table
Make it a multi-cluster warehouse with a higher MAX_CLUSTER_COUNT
Increase the warehouse from Small to 2X-Large
blocks.explain: Queuing under many small queries is a concurrency problem, solved by more clusters. A bigger single cluster mainly speeds up individual heavy queries.

blocks.q: A query shows 'partitions scanned: 48,000 of 50,000' with a filter on customer_id. What does it indicate?
options: Pruning is ineffective because customer_id values are spread across almost all micro-partitions
blocks.explain: Scanned versus total micro-partitions measures pruning. Nearly all scanned means the column is not clustered; warehouse size changes speed, not the number of partitions read.

blocks.q: Which statement about zero-copy cloning is correct?
options: It is only available for transient tables
It disables time travel on the source table
It copies all micro-partitions into new storage immediately
The clone shares micro-partitions with the source, and storage grows only as either side changes
blocks.explain: Cloning is metadata-only. New storage appears as data diverges. It works for databases, schemas and tables and does not affect the source's time travel.

blocks.q: A dropped permanent table had a 1-day retention. Ten days later, what recovery options exist?
options: None: it is past both time travel (1 day) and fail-safe (7 days)
blocks.explain: After 1 day of time travel and 7 days of fail-safe the data is gone. Within fail-safe, only Snowflake support can recover data; users cannot query or clone it.
